Filter methods

Source: vignettes/articles/filters.Rmd
filters.Rmd

A filter scores each feature with a statistic and keeps the features whose score passes a cut. No predictive model is fitted, so filters are the cheapest methods in featR and the usual first step on wide data. Each one is univariate: it judges every feature on its own, so it cannot see redundancy between features or effects that only appear in combination.

featR has five filters, and they split by whether they look at the outcome:

  • fs_unsupervised() and fs_correlation() never touch the outcome. You can run them before a train/test split.
  • fs_supervised(), fs_chi(), and fs_infogain() score features against the outcome. Selecting with them is part of fitting the model, so run them on training rows only, or inside every fold of a cross-validation.

None of the filters reports a held-out performance number. Their scores are statistics on whatever rows you pass in. Validation and leakage shows how much a filter run on all the data inflates a later cross-validation estimate, and lists which numbers in featR are honest.

The examples use one simulated data set, so the right answers are known in advance:

set.seed(1)
n <- 200
sim <- data.frame(
  x_strong = rnorm(n),
  x_weak   = rnorm(n),
  x_noise  = rnorm(n),
  x_const  = 5,
  x_gappy  = ifelse(runif(n) < 0.6, NA, rnorm(n))
)
sim$x_copy <- sim$x_strong + rnorm(n, sd = 0.05)   # near-duplicate
sim$y      <- 2 * sim$x_strong + 0.5 * sim$x_weak + rnorm(n)
sim$class  <- factor(ifelse(sim$y > 0, "pos", "neg"))

Filters that ignore the outcome

fs_unsupervised()

fs_unsupervised() scores each column by a statistic that needs no outcome: "variance" (the default), "mad", "iqr", "range", "missing_prop", or "n_unique". Use it to drop constant columns, columns that are mostly missing, or columns with too few distinct values. Every column of data must be numeric.

With the defaults (method = "variance", threshold = 0), it keeps every column whose variance is above zero, which drops the constant ones.

num <- sim[, c("x_strong", "x_weak", "x_noise", "x_const", "x_copy")]
fs_unsupervised(num, method = "variance", threshold = 0)
#> <fs_result> unsupervised_variance
#> Selected 4 of 5 features
#>   x_strong, x_weak, x_noise, x_copy
#> Details: mask, indices, filtered, threshold, direction, action, n_features (in $details)

To drop columns that are more than half missing, you have to say action = "remove":

fs_unsupervised(sim[, c("x_strong", "x_gappy")], method = "missing_prop",
                threshold = 0.5, action = "remove")$selected
#> [1] "x_strong"

With the default action = "keep", the same call would keep the most missing columns. featR warns when you use "missing_prop" with all three of threshold, direction, and action at their defaults, because that combination keeps every column with any missing value.

Thresholds are on the scale of the statistic. A variance is in squared units, "missing_prop" is a proportion in [0, 1], and "n_unique" is a count, so a threshold chosen for one method means nothing for another. "mad" uses R’s default consistency constant (1.4826), so for normally distributed data it estimates the standard deviation rather than giving the raw median absolute deviation.

On missing values: na_rm = TRUE (the default) drops them before computing "variance", "mad", "iqr", and "range". "missing_prop" and "n_unique" always count the whole column. A column whose score comes out NA is never selected, and a warning says how many were excluded.

A high variance says nothing about usefulness. A noisy column can have the largest variance in the data and a strong predictor the smallest, so use this function for clean-up, not for ranking.

fs_correlation()

fs_correlation() looks only at how the features relate to each other. It flags every pair whose absolute correlation is above threshold (which has no default), and with prune = TRUE (the default) it drops features one at a time until no two survivors are above it. In sim, x_copy is x_strong plus a little noise:

red <- fs_correlation(num[, c("x_strong", "x_weak", "x_noise", "x_copy")],
                      threshold = 0.9)
red$selected
#> [1] "x_strong" "x_weak"   "x_noise"
red$details$dropped
#> [1] "x_copy"
red$details$pairs
#>       Var1   Var2 Correlation
#> 1 x_strong x_copy   0.9984364

The pair correlates at 0.998, and one member goes. Each step takes the strongest remaining pair and drops the member with the larger mean absolute correlation to the other retained features. That is the tie-break caret::findCorrelation() uses, but caret scans in a different order, so the two can drop different features. Neither is guaranteed to drop the fewest.

The choice never consults the outcome, so it can drop the member that predicts better. Here it dropped x_copy and kept x_strong, but it could as easily have gone the other way. If the choice inside a correlated group should follow importance for a target, use fs_boruta() instead.

Reading the result:

  • scores holds each feature’s largest absolute correlation with any other feature.
  • With prune = FALSE, selected is the redundant set (both members of every flagged pair) and nothing is dropped. details$redundant holds that set in either mode.

The correlation types are "pearson" (the default), "spearman", "kendall", "polychoric" (all columns ordered factors; needs the polycor package), and "pointbiserial" (a continuous column against a column with exactly two values).

Missing values are not removed by default (na.rm = FALSE). An NA in a column makes its correlations NA, and pairs with an NA correlation are never flagged or pruned, so redundancy you cannot see is treated as none. featR warns when this happens. Set na.rm = TRUE for pairwise deletion, or casewise deletion under "polychoric", which stops with an error on missing values otherwise.

Filters that score against the outcome

fs_supervised()

fs_supervised() scores every feature against target, and every feature column must be numeric. For a numeric target the score is the absolute Pearson correlation, in [0, 1]. For a factor, character, or logical target it is the one-way ANOVA F statistic, which has no upper bound. The default method = "auto" picks between them from the target’s type.

reg <- sim[, c("x_strong", "x_weak", "x_noise", "x_copy", "y")]
res <- fs_supervised(reg, target = "y", threshold = 0.2)
summary(res)
#> <fs_result> supervised_correlation (regression)
#> Selected 2 of 4 features
#>   x_strong, x_copy
#> Details: mask, indices, filtered, threshold, direction, action, n_features (in $details)
#> 
#> Call:
#>   fs_supervised(data = reg, target = "y", threshold = 0.2)
#> 
#> Scores (4 features, ranked):
#>   feature   score selected
#>  x_strong 0.85750        *
#>    x_copy 0.85560        *
#>    x_weak 0.17000         
#>   x_noise 0.05669         
#> (* = selected)

x_copy scores 0.856, almost the same as x_strong, and is kept even though it adds nothing once x_strong is in. Every univariate filter behaves this way. Run fs_correlation() afterwards to prune the duplicate.

x_weak has a real effect (coefficient 0.5) but scores 0.17 and falls below the cut. The default threshold = 0 would have kept all four features: any non-constant feature has a sample correlation above zero, even pure noise. Choose a threshold to make an actual selection.

For a factor target, choose the threshold on the F scale:

cls <- sim[, c("x_strong", "x_weak", "x_noise", "class")]
fs_supervised(cls, target = "class", threshold = 10)$scores
#>    x_strong      x_weak     x_noise 
#> 141.5738542   5.4736576   0.2682509

x_strong scores 141.6, and x_weak (5.5) and x_noise (0.27) fall below 10. A feature that separates the classes perfectly scores Inf.

Caveats:

  • The task in the result is "regression" for a numeric target and "classification" for a factor. A character or logical target is scored with ANOVA, but the task is recorded as NA.
  • Pearson correlation and the F test measure a linear relationship or a difference in class means. A feature with a strong U-shaped effect can score near zero; the fs_infogain() section below shows one.
  • With na_rm = TRUE (the default), each feature is scored on the rows where both it and the target are observed. A constant feature has no defined score; it scores NA and is never selected.

fs_chi()

fs_chi() runs a chi-squared test of independence between each categorical feature and the target. Character columns become factors. Numeric, logical, and date columns are ignored, so discretize them first if you want them tested. The target is coerced to a factor too, and the task is always "classification".

cat_data <- data.frame(
  color = factor(ifelse(sim$x_strong > 0, "red", "blue")),
  size  = factor(sample(c("S", "M", "L"), n, replace = TRUE)),
  class = sim$class
)
chi <- fs_chi(cat_data, target = "class", seed = 1)
chi$selected
#> [1] "color"
chi$details$results
#>   feature   n df      p_value  adj_p_value significant     method
#> 1   color 200  1 3.090128e-16 6.180256e-16        TRUE asymptotic
#> 2    size 200  2 6.356383e-01 1.000000e+00       FALSE asymptotic
#>   correction_applied min_expected
#> 1               TRUE        43.24
#> 2              FALSE        25.76

color is a coarsened copy of x_strong, and its adjusted p-value is about 6e-16. size is random and gets an adjusted p-value of 1.

The score for each feature is its adjusted p-value, so smaller means stronger evidence of association, and summary() sorts the scores ascending. A feature is selected when its adjusted p-value is below sig_level (default 0.05). The adjustment is Bonferroni by default (p_adjust_method), counting only the features that were actually tested.

When every expected cell count is at least 5, the test is the usual asymptotic one, with Yates’ continuity correction on 2x2 tables (the correction_applied column). When any expected count is below 5, the p-value comes from a Monte Carlo simulation with simulation_B = 2000 replicates and df is NA. Pass seed to make those p-values reproducible. A simulated p-value can never fall below 1 / (simulation_B + 1), so with many features and a Bonferroni correction it may be unable to reach sig_level at all; featR warns and says how large simulation_B would need to be.

Each feature is tested on its own complete cases, so n can differ between rows of the results table. A feature or target left with fewer than two levels after dropping missing values is skipped, with an NA p-value.

A p-value measures evidence against independence. It is not an effect size: with enough rows, a negligible association is still significant.

fs_infogain()

fs_infogain() scores each feature by its information gain, H(Y) - H(Y | X): how many bits of uncertainty about the target you lose by knowing the feature. It accepts numeric, factor, character, logical, and date features in the same data frame, and it does not assume a linear relationship.

ig <- fs_infogain(sim[, c("x_strong", "x_weak", "x_noise", "class")],
                  target = "class")
ig$scores
#>   x_strong     x_weak    x_noise 
#> 0.41907995 0.11210176 0.05730707

The target is always treated as categorical, and the task is always "classification". Numeric features are cut into equal-width bins, using the larger of the Freedman-Diaconis and Sturges bin counts unless you set numeric_bins. A numeric target is binned the same way, once and up front, so every feature is scored against the same classes. Date columns are expanded into year, month, and day columns. Missing values are dropped pair by pair, never across the whole data set.

Because it bins rather than fitting a line, information gain catches the U-shaped effect that fs_supervised() misses:

set.seed(2)
u <- data.frame(x_u = rnorm(n), x_lin = rnorm(n))
u$y <- u$x_u^2 + 0.3 * u$x_lin + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
fs_supervised(u, target = "y")$scores
#>        x_u      x_lin 
#> 0.04566085 0.36929494
fs_infogain(u, target = "y")$scores
#>       x_u     x_lin 
#> 1.2513951 0.6727366

x_u drives most of y, yet its absolute correlation is 0.05 against 0.37 for x_lin. Information gain ranks it first, 1.25 bits against 0.67.

Raw information gain favors features with many levels. An identifier column splits the data into single rows and reaches the largest gain possible, while predicting nothing about new data. normalize = "gain_ratio" divides each gain by the feature’s own entropy, which grows with the number of levels:

with_id <- cbind(id = factor(seq_len(n)), sim[, c("x_strong", "class")])
fs_infogain(with_id, "class")$scores
#>        id  x_strong 
#> 0.9953784 0.4190800
fs_infogain(with_id, "class", normalize = "gain_ratio")$scores
#>        id  x_strong 
#> 0.1302194 0.1285049

The gain ratio cuts the ID column’s score from 1.00 to 0.13, roughly a factor of eight, but on this data the ID column still ranks first (0.130 against 0.129 for x_strong). The gain ratio reduces the bias toward many levels without removing it, so drop identifier and other near-unique columns before you score anything. Gain ratios are not on the bits scale, so a threshold chosen for raw gains does not carry over.

By default selected holds every feature with a score above zero. With finite data, almost every feature has some positive sample gain, including pure noise, so the default selects nearly everything. Use top_n to keep a fixed number of the highest-scoring features.

data can also be a list of data frames that share the target column. The scores are then the union across the list, and a feature name that appears in more than one data frame keeps its highest score; details$collisions records which.
